The central question is whether gradient updates that improve a model's performance on capability tasks (e.g., coding, reasoning) systematically point in directions that degrade alignment properties (e.g., refusal of harmful requests, calibrated uncertainty), and if so, whether standard multi-task loss weighting can resolve this or whether the conflict is geometrically fundamental. The key concepts are the loss landscape as a high-dimensional manifold, gradient conflict (when ∇L_capability · ∇L_alignment < 0, meaning the two gradients have negative dot product and any step that helps one hurts the other), Pareto-optimal fronts in loss space, and the distinction between gradient interference (occasional conflict, resolvable by projection methods like PCGrad or MGDA) versus gradient opposition (systematic conflict along critical directions, not resolvable without architectural or data-level intervention). A beginner assumes that because both objectives are expressed as cross-entropy over token distributions, they live in the same "space" and can be smoothly traded off with a scalar weight λ — an expert knows that the curvature of the loss surface differs sharply between objectives, so a step that crosses a flat region for capability may traverse a sharp ridge for alignment, making the effective trade-off wildly sensitive to learning rate and batch composition in ways no fixed λ captures. The deeper worry is that alignment properties may occupy low-measure, high-curvature basins that are catastrophically easy to exit during capability fine-tuning, while being very hard to re-enter — meaning alignment degradation can be sudden, large, and poorly signaled by aggregate loss metrics that are dominated by the capability objective.

This breaks down in the alignment-capability case because alignment loss surfaces are empirically highly anisotropic: the work on loss landscape geometry from Henighan et al. and the "sharpness-aware" literature shows that RLHF-tuned models sit in basins with orders-of-magnitude difference in curvature across directions, meaning the "neutral plane" PCGrad projects onto is not actually neutral — it may still climb steeply along a sharp alignment ridge. Concretely, Anthropic's and DeepMind's internal evals (and published proxy results from the Llama-2 and Mistral alignment ablations) show that even small-norm gradient steps during SFT capability tuning can move a model 10-30% of the way toward pre-alignment behavior on refusal benchmarks, which is inconsistent with PCGrad's implicit claim that projected updates are alignment-safe. The result is that PCGrad and MGDA both address acute gradient conflict but are blind to chronic, low-signal alignment erosion — exactly the failure mode that matters most operationally.

Adam's second-moment estimator v̂_t is an exponential moving average of squared gradients, which means it accumulates a "memory" of which parameter directions have been active; for capability gradients that fire densely every step, v̂_t grows large and stable along those directions, while for alignment gradients that fire rarely, v̂_t remains small along their directions until an alignment example arrives. The critical interaction is that Adam's effective learning rate for parameter direction i is η/√v̂_i — so when an alignment gradient finally fires, v̂_i is small for alignment-specific directions (no recent history), which should naively increase the effective step size there, but the problem is the opposite for shared directions: along parameter axes that capability training has made large in v̂_t, the alignment gradient component in those directions is heavily damped, and since capability and alignment updates share many high-level representational parameters, this damping is pervasive. Concretely, Kosson et al. (2023) and related work on Adam's implicit bias show that dense-gradient directions accumulate preconditioner mass that crowds out sparse-gradient directions in shared parameter subspaces, effectively implementing a frequency-weighted priority that is blind to the functional importance of rare updates. The practical consequence, visible in fine-tuning runs of models like Llama-2-chat where alignment was measured via HarmBench pass rates during continued SFT, is that alignment degradation is not uniform but concentrated in exactly the shared representational layers where Adam's preconditioner is most dominated by capability gradient history — the optimizer itself becomes a structural amplifier of the gradient conflict problem.

The ROME/MEMIT line of work is more damning for post-hoc restoration: factual associations edited into mid-layer MLP weights interact with attention patterns in downstream layers in ways that cannot be predicted from the edit alone, and alignment suppression almost certainly has the same property — the suppression is not just a vector added to the residual stream but a pattern of attention routing that prevents certain token interactions from completing, which is a multiplicative, context-dependent operation, not an additive one. Mechanistically, this is why "re-adding the RLHF delta" experiments (subtracting a base model from its aligned version and adding that delta to a capability-fine-tuned model) recover only partial alignment — Ilharco et al.'s task arithmetic work shows that delta addition works well for independent capabilities but degrades roughly proportionally to the degree of shared parameter support, which for alignment versus capability is high. Inference-time steering vectors are fundamentally a residual stream intervention — you add a fixed direction to activations at specified layers and positions — which means they can only directly manipulate the additive component of alignment, leaving the attention routing component untouched. The context-dependence of alignment-relevant routing is precisely what makes this inadequate as a substitute: a steering vector that successfully suppresses harmful completions on the prompt distribution used to derive it will fail on prompts that activate different attention circuits, because the routing patterns that need to be suppressed are different, and no single fixed vector addresses all of them. Turner et al.'s activation addition work (2023) demonstrates this concretely — their steering vectors achieve strong behavioral modification on in-distribution prompts but show degradation and unexpected side effects (incoherence, topic bleed) on out-of-distribution prompts, which is the signature of a fixed additive intervention colliding with context-dependent routing it wasn't derived from. The numbers from representation engineering (Zou et al.) reinforce this: linear probes for alignment-relevant concepts achieve 85-95% accuracy at the layer they're extracted from, but cross-layer and cross-context transfer drops to 60-75%, meaning the "direction" is not actually fixed — it's a local approximation to something that curves through activation space with context. The deeper issue is that training-time alignment shapes the weights — the routing matrices themselves — while inference-time steering only perturbs activations, so any sufficiently adversarial prompt that routes through circuits the steering vector doesn't cover can bypass it entirely, which is exactly the threat model that matters for safety. This means steering vectors are best understood as a diagnostic and interpretability tool, or a soft behavioral nudge for well-characterized distributions, not a safety primitive — using them as a substitute for training-time alignment is like patching a compromised kernel from userspace.

Prakash et al. and the path patching methodology from mechanistic interpretability (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023) provide operational tools here: by intervening on specific (layer, head, token-position) triples and measuring downstream behavioral change, you can identify which heads carry alignment-critical routing — empirically this turns out to be a small fraction of total heads, often in middle layers, with some models showing ~5-15% of heads responsible for >80% of refusal-relevant routing. The distinguishing signature is therefore whether the MLP weight update ΔW produces output changes that are aligned with existing residual stream directions (knowledge encoding — adding new content along directions the model already uses) versus transverse to existing residual stream directions (routing-destructive — introducing novel directions that perturb downstream QK inner products in ways the attention heads weren't trained to handle). This suggests a concrete detection signal: for each MLP update ΔW, compute the projection of ΔW·x onto the subspace spanned by the alignment-sensitive attention heads' key vectors at that layer (derivable from the routing sensitivity mask discussed previously), and flag updates where this projection exceeds a threshold as routing-risk updates — empirically this would require maintaining a ~d×k matrix of alignment-sensitive key directions, where k is the number of flagged heads, which is computationally cheap relative to the forward pass. The problem is that this detection is prompt-distribution-dependent: whether ΔW·x is transverse to alignment-critical directions depends on x, and capability fine-tuning necessarily introduces new x distributions (the new task's inputs), so the MLP update may be safe on the training distribution while being routing-destructive on the alignment-probe distribution that wasn't present during the step. Daheim et al.'s work on continual learning interference (2023) quantifies a related phenomenon: MLP updates during task fine-tuning cause "silent" degradation on held-out tasks at a rate roughly proportional to the cosine distance between the new task's input distribution and the held-out task's, suggesting a practical early-warning signal — monitor cosine distance between capability fine-tuning batch representations and alignment probe representations at each MLP layer, and treat large distance as a proxy for routing-destruction risk before it compounds into measurable behavioral degradation.
